newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Brash tells exporters NZ at watershed - sources.
newsitem.headline: Brash tells exporters NZ at watershed - sources.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash told an exporters' conference the economy was at a turning point and a loosening of monetary policy was around the corner, sources from the closed meeting said on Tuesday.
"The key thing he said was that we are at a turning point in the cycle, and for him to say that, that's relatively significant," one source who declined to be named said.
Brash and RBNZ Deputy Governor Murray Sherwin attended the meeting.

Brash's only comments to the media were that the New Zealand dollar was near the peak of its cycle and that he was attending the meeting as recognition of the pressure exporters were under because of the strong currency.

"They (the RBNZ) obviously believe that next year inflation will come down, interest rates will come down and that will take some of the pressure off the New Zealand dollar in nominal and real terms. So they believe they will get a flat to falling exchange rate," the source said.
Brash was careful not to indicate if there would be an easing in the bank's Monetary Policy Statement on December 17.
One source said he interpreted from what he heard that policy would be loosened "but that will depend pretty significantly on what the new government is".

The New Zealand First Party, which has held the balance of power since the October 12 election, is in talks with the caretaker National government and left-leaning Labour Party about forming a coalition. Parties are trying to clinch a deal before parliament meets next Thursday.

Sherwin told the meeting that monetary settings were currently based on the assumption that a NZ$1.1 billion second round of tax cuts, or their fiscal equivalent, will be introduced in 1997 after a first round this year.
"He's basically observing that financial markets are already anticipating a worse fiscal outcome than the RB assumption and that's already embedded in rates today," the source said.
So Sherwin suggested that if the fiscal policy is slacker than what we already know, then financial markets might not react too badly to it, the source said.

Asked at the meeting what would happen if the tax cuts were to be abandoned, as Brash suggested last month may need to happen, Sherwin agreed that that would lead to quite a sharp loosening of monetary policy.
"That would mean the bank's fiscal assumptions are wrong and in fact fiscal conditions would be even tighter than they anticipated," a source said.
Brash recognised that fiscal policies to date had helped the bank's anti-inflationary drive.
"If the tax cuts were abandoned then it would be even greater assistance to monetary conditions -- therefore they (monetary conditions) could be slackened," this source said.
Brash and Sherwin told the meeting that although short-term interest rates had fallen nearly 150 basis points since the October 12 election, the NZ dollar had actually gone up.

A loosening of monetary policy would not guarantee the New Zealand dollar would fall, they said. Sherwin pointed to the situation in Australia, where interest rates had been cut twice this year but the Australian dollar had gone up.

Some flexibility with respect to achieving the bank's 0-2 percent inflation target was in practice how monetary policy was being set now, Brash told the meeting. The bank has been at the top of or outside its target range throughout this year.
He said that was pretty much the same as what Labour and NZ First were asking for.
"He basically indicated that the 0-2 percent inflation target was up for grabs in the polical bunfight that was going on," said one source.
"Brash indicated there would be no great change to operational parts of Reserve Bank policy even though the bands might be widened."
Brash repeated there were certain government policies which could help the fight against inflation, such as opening up accident insurance to competition.
The suggestion this week by Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen of a reintroduction of a foreign withholding tax on bonds was apparently rejected.
Brash said foreign companies found their way around such measures. But Brash said he recognised exporters' problems.

"He fully recognised the current state of monetary policy was harming exports and he was pretty honest that it was a blunt instrument but he could see few ways of sharpening it," the source said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
